recent_posts.title: Why nobody is learning C++ in 2026
Two career paths for software developers in the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: AI is automating the 'middle layer' of software development — CRUD apps, basic APIs, glue code — putting junior and mid-level developers at risk. Two viable career paths remain for senior engineers: becoming an AI orchestrator who directs AI systems, or going lower down the stack into systems programming. The author argues systems programming is the stronger long-term bet due to zero error tolerance, strict regulatory requirements (e.g., DO-178C for aerospace), and legal accountability that AI cannot satisfy. Rust is highlighted as the language of choice for this transition, with adoption by Microsoft, AWS, Google, and the Linux kernel. The post ends with a pitch for a paid Rust training program called the Rust Live Accelerator.

recent_posts.title: Four Rust career paths and how to choose the right one
recent_posts.summary: A breakdown of four main Rust career paths: backend/web services, systems programming/infrastructure, embedded IoT/robotics, and developer tooling. Each path is covered with typical day-to-day work, salary ranges (from ~$100K for mid-level backend to $400K+ for senior systems roles), required skills, and guidance on which path fits different backgrounds. Backend is recommended as the fastest entry point for most developers, while systems programming offers the highest pay but longest ramp-up. The post concludes with a pitch for a structured Rust mentorship program.

recent_posts.title: Why learning Rust will ruin you for every other language
recent_posts.summary: A satirical, reverse-psychology piece arguing against learning Rust by listing its 'downsides' — all of which are actually strengths. The compiler catches bugs at compile time, the Option type forces explicit null handling, refactoring is safe, the community is deeply educational, and Rust job demand keeps growing in safety-critical domains. The piece ends with a pitch for a 'Rust Live Accelerator' training program.

recent_posts.title: Understanding Rust's advanced features through async trait objects
recent_posts.summary: Rust's advanced features like trait objects, async/await, pinning, Send/Sync bounds, and lifetimes are explained through building a user service interface. The tutorial walks through compiler errors that arise when combining dynamic dispatch with async methods, explaining why async functions aren't trait-object compatible by default, how futures work as state machines, why pinning prevents memory unsafety in self-referential types, how Send/Sync traits enable thread safety, and how lifetime annotations tie reference validity together. The complexity is ultimately simplified using the async-trait macro.

recent_posts.title: Three strategies for learning Rust more effectively
recent_posts.summary: Three key strategies for learning Rust more effectively: focus on domain-specific knowledge rather than trying to master every feature, maintain consistent progress through community support and mentorship instead of repeatedly restarting, and learn with the goal of becoming job-market ready to ensure practical skill development. The approach emphasizes learning only the 20% of Rust needed for your specific use case, whether backend services, embedded systems, or blockchain development.

recent_posts.title: Rust is now officially part of the Linux Kernel
recent_posts.summary: Rust has been officially recognized as a core language in the Linux kernel, moving beyond its three-year experimental phase. At a recent Linux kernel maintainer summit, top maintainers including Linus Torvalds confirmed zero pushback on this decision. While the kernel contains 34 million lines of C versus 25,000 lines of Rust, this official status validates Rust for systems programming and opens career opportunities for developers skilled in both C and Rust. The move represents a significant milestone, as Rust succeeded where C++ previously failed in gaining kernel adoption.

recent_posts.title: Rust approaches mainstream adoption crossover in 2026
recent_posts.summary: Rust stands at a critical juncture in 2026, positioned to either cross into mainstream adoption or fade into niche use. Major tech companies like AWS, Google, and Microsoft are already using Rust for critical infrastructure, and the language excels in tooling with Cargo and mature frameworks. However, the talent pool remains limited, with companies struggling to find competent Rust developers. The bull case centers on Rust's unique ability to provide memory safety without sacrificing performance, making it essential for critical systems. The bear case argues that most companies don't need Rust's guarantees and that developer productivity matters more. With growing demand in AI infrastructure, robotics, and embedded systems, learning Rust now could position developers advantageously before the talent market becomes saturated.

recent_posts.title: 21 rust development tips from debugging to production systems
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide covering 21+ Rust development techniques across three skill levels. Covers debugging tools like the debug macro and Cargo Bacon for faster feedback loops, scaling strategies including traits, generics, macros, and workspace organization, and senior-level practices like type-driven design, the type state pattern, and CI/CD tooling with Clippy, Cargo Audit, and Cargo Deny. Emphasizes compiler-driven development and making invalid states unrepresentable through Rust's type system.

recent_posts.title: How a TikTok intern saved $300K by rewriting Go services in Rust
recent_posts.summary: A TikTok intern rewrote CPU-intensive payment service endpoints from Go to Rust, reducing average latency by 30%, P99 latency by 76%, and cutting compute costs by 50%—saving $300K annually. The migration used a gradual rollout strategy with separate Rust clusters under the same service name, avoiding upstream code changes. Key challenges included adapting Go's zero values to Rust's Option enum and optimizing memory allocations. The main lesson: Rust delivers performance gains at the cost of developer productivity, making it ideal for high-usage, stable components where economies of scale justify the rewrite effort.
